headline: Newport to Napatree: Peanuts Pour the Rocks, Albies Pick the Breachways
subhead: Full moon tide has bait balled tight from Brenton Point to Napatree, and the first real blitz signs are showing before the new moon even arrives.
body_markdown:
Walk any rock pile from Brenton Point to Napatree right now and you'll see it before you cast a line — peanut bunker pouring off the ledges in nervous sheets, getting pushed tight against the granite by anything with teeth. Bay anchovies and silversides are doing the same dance in the breachways, and that combination is exactly what turns this stretch of coast on in September. The full moon that came through September 6-7 did what we said it would do last week — it's tightened those bait schools hard, and the first legitimate blitz behavior of the fall is starting to show up in pieces, not yet coastwide, but building.

Water's sitting in that comfortable high-60s window — Newport-area readings are tracking close to what Narragansett Bay and eastern Long Island Sound are showing, high 60s to low 70s depending on the day and the tide stage, which is right where albies and bass both want to be. That's not blow-your-hair-back warm, but it's stable, and stable water with tightening bait is the pattern that matters more than any single number on a buoy.

Striped bass are in full staging mode. Bunker schools that have been loose and scattered through the bay all summer are balling up as the moon pulls harder tides through the passages, and that bait is starting to spill out of Narragansett Bay onto the south-facing beaches — Second Beach in Middletown, the stretch off Sachuest, down through Matunuck. Fish are working those schools but it's still more pick than blitz most days — a few bass busting on the surface at first light, then going quiet once the sun gets up. The bunker run this stretch has been waiting on is close. Expect that to change fast once the new moon tide arrives September 10 and really starts moving water — that's the pivot point to watch.

Albies are the story of the week on the ocean side. They pushed into the breachways first — Charlestown Breachway and the Weekapaug/Watch Hill corridor are holding fish on the last two hours of the ebb, when bait gets funneled out through the cut and stacks up against the current seam. Napatree's outer bar is doing the same thing on a bigger scale — fish working the rip where the sandbar drops into deeper water, especially on the last of the outgoing into the start of the new flood. These fish are keying on tiny bay anchovies right now, not the bigger peanut bunker the stripers are chasing, so profile matters. Half-ounce to 3/4-ounce epoxy jigs in bay anchovy colors — olive over white, sometimes just clear/silver — are outfishing the bigger Deceivers and Albie Snax that worked earlier in the run. If the fish are up and showing but refusing, go smaller before you go faster.

Bluefish are mixed into both bites, and they're not shy about it — anywhere the bunker or anchovies are getting worked over, there's a decent chance a few choppers show up and shred a topwater plug or a bucktail meant for something else. Not a bad problem to have if you're using wire or heavier leader, which you should be doing right now anyway given how thick the blues are running.

Tautog fishing is still a step behind the calendar. The ledges are holding fish — the usual spots off Jamestown's Beavertail rocks, the drop-offs around Castle Hill, the rock piles off Sakonnet Point — but the real green crab bite doesn't turn serious until the water cools another few degrees and those fish tuck into the cracks for the fall push. Right now it's a slack-tide proposition on the deeper humps, worth a stop if you're already out there for albies, not yet worth building a whole trip around.

Fluke are winding down, as expected this time of year. The drifts off Jamestown and outside Newport Harbor are still giving up keeper fish on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the bottom on the last of the incoming, but the window is closing fast as those fish start their move offshore. Scup are still thick around the same rock structure that holds the tog, easy pickings on squid strips if you want a bucket of dinner fish between blitz windows.

The Sakonnet shore is fishing on its own clock compared to the south-facing beaches. Bait gets funneled down through the East Passage and piles up around the point on a stage of tide that doesn't match what's happening at Second Beach or Matunuck — worth checking both if the first spot's dead, because they rarely go quiet at the same time.

Look at the next few days as the setup, not the show. If the wind stays out of the north and northwest and lets the water lay down, the breachways should keep producing albies on the ebb, and bass should keep picking at bunker on the beaches at first and last light. But the real trigger is that new moon tide on the 10th — if bunker density in the bay keeps spilling south the way it has been, this is the week the first true blitz of the fall should break loose somewhere between Sachuest and Napatree. Keep the light gear rigged for albies and something heavier in reserve for when the bass finally decide to show up in numbers.
